raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old Caucasian male was referred to our Department of Ophthalmology for sudden decreased visual acuity, initially in the right eye, followed after two weeks by the left eye. The patient was treated in another medical service with methylprednisolone intravenously followed by oral therapy, but without a favorable clinical response. He was addressed to our clinic, one month after the sudden onset of the visual loss in the right eye. The patient had no medical history of diseases.
On ophthalmologic examination, he had a visual acuity of 20/ 400 in both eyes. The intraocular pressure of the right and left eye was 20 mmHg GAT and 18 mmHg GAT, respectively. The anterior segment of both eyes had a normal appearance on slit-lamp examination and normal direct and consensual pupillary light reflexes and the absence of a relative afferent pupillary defect were also noted. 
Fundus examination (Fig. 1,2) demonstrated bilateral protruding, hyperemic, with blurred margins in the nasal quadrant papilla and reduced excavation, tortuous vessels, peripapillary telangiectasias. 
The OCT revealed bilateral increase of the RNFL thickness (Fig. 3) and GCL-IPL complex severely thinned (Fig. 4).
Based on the anamnesis, the ophthalmological examination, and the OCT examination, the first stage diagnosis was optic neuritis in both eyes. In order of importance, different causes of bilateral papillary edema in a young adult [] were taken into consideration. Intracranial expansive processes, as tumors, hemorrhages, hematomas and pseudotumor cerebri, were excluded by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan. Nearby inflammatory processes, such as sinus or dental, were excluded from the anamnesis and MRI scan. Infectious processes, like syphilis, were excluded by paraclinical investigations. We excluded arteritic [] and non-arteritic [] anterior ischemic optic neuropathies due to absent blood dyscrasias in our patient and the age segment of which he is part. We have also excluded multiple sclerosis and optic nerve and orbit tumors that rarely cause bilateral damage. Last, but not least, we considered LHON, which was confirmed by genetic testing three weeks later.
Subsequently, the administrative procedures for obtaining the treatment with idebenone were initiated and treatment was started four months later after the presentation. The patient administrated idebenone as recommended by the producer (300 mg T.I.D.). At the time of initiation of idebenone treatment, the visual acuity decreased to counting fingers (CF) in both eyes, the intraocular pressure of the right and left eye was 19 mmHg GAT, and pupillary reflexes were normal. Fundus examination at initiation of treatment (Fig. 5,6) revealed plane papilla, with net contour, pale and small excavation at both eyes. The vessels had normal caliber and route. The OCT examination of the optic nerve revealed a normal thickness of RNFL (Fig. 7), except for the temporal quadrants, where the thickness was low. Regarding the GCL-IPL complex (Fig. 8), an emphasis of the thickness decrease compared to the moment of presentation was noticed. Perimetry at initiation of the idebenone treatment (Fig. 9) showed an overall reduction in the sensitivity of the nerve fibers with absolute scotoma in the centrocecal area.
From the initiation of treatment, the patient was reevaluated at every three months (at three, six, nine, and twelve months). None of the reevaluations showed any improvement of the visual acuity. The fundoscopy (Fig. 10) aspect remained the same from the initiation of treatment. Three months after treatment initiation, the OCT assessment of the optic nerve revealed progression of atrophy in all quadrants, except for the nasal quadrants, which were spared. At six, nine, and twelve months, we found a stationary look (Fig. 11). The OCT assessment of the GCL-IPL complex (Fig. 12) revealed a stable appearance. As it was observed, there was an improvement at the perimetric evaluation (Fig. 13), the discreet reduction of the scotoma in periphery, but unnoticed by the patient.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old Caucasian male presented 1 month after sudden painless visual loss in his right eye followed 2 weeks later by sudden visual loss in his left eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One month prior to referral, the patient experienced acute painless visual decline in the right eye, followed 2 weeks later by identical visual loss in the left eye. Intravenous and oral methylprednisolone therapy at an outside hospital for presumed bilateral optic neuritis yielded no improvement.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for sequential painless severe bilateral visual loss. Recent medication: intravenous and oral methylprednisolone.

objective.physical_examination: At presentation (1 month after onset), visual acuity was 20/400 OU (subsequently declining to counting fingers OU at month 4), intraocular pressures were 20 mmHg OD and 18 mmHg OS, anterior segments were normal, and pupillary light reflexes were preserved without RAPD. Initial fundoscopy demonstrated bilateral hyperemic, protruding optic discs with blurred nasal margins, tortuous retinal vessels, and peripapillary telangiectatic microangiopathy; by month 4, fundoscopy showed bilateral flat, pale, atrophic optic discs.
objective.routine_investigations: Paraclinical infectious and hematologic investigations including syphilis testing were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline OCT showed bilateral peripapillary RNFL pseudo-edema/thickening with severe thinning of the macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer (GCL-IPL) complex, which progressed over 3-4 months to diffuse optic atrophy and severe centrocecal absolute scotomas on automated perimetry. Brain and orbital MRI was normal, excluding compressive, demyelinating (MS), or sinus pathology. Mitochondrial genetic testing confirmed Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Confirmed Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) by genetic testing after excluding infectious optic neuropathies (including syphilis), demyelinating optic neuritis, and intracranial masses. Treated starting 4 months after presentation with oral idebenone 300 mg three times daily; over 12 months of quarterly follow-up, visual acuity remained at counting fingers OU with stable GCL-IPL thickness on OCT and a subtle peripheral reduction of the centrocecal scotoma on perimetry.
